semantic_rust_review.message: 语义审查（Rust）判定本次改动有缺陷；overall_severity 分数越高问题越重（warn>=1 / fail>=2），具体类目判定见 finding 的 extra 字段。按 15 类目核对 diff（事实卡驱动：name_behavior / comment_rubric / placement / clone_necessity / cleanliness_semantics 对着每项的 FACT CARD 判决）：typos / name_behavior / comment_rubric / placement / clone_necessity / cleanliness_semantics / ownership_lifetime / error_panic / unsafe_boundaries / concurrency / async_cancellation / collections_perf / type_api_design / macros / security；确认无问题后书面驳回。
semantic_rust_review.intent: Rust code review against the OpenCodeReview semantic rubric (internal/config/rules/rule_docs/rust.md). Judge the CHANGED Rust code (not the whole file) against each category; a finding is one of the listed conditions actually present in the diff, not a style preference. Favor precision over recall: report only defects likely real; correctness/security findings are blocking, style-only are advisory. Use file_read/code_search context to establish call sites, ownership, and boundaries before claiming a non-local defect; do not infer defects from a function name alone. Before reporting any non-local claim, establish the call site, ownership, synchronization, and trust boundary from the diff and provided context; report a finding only on concrete evidence actually present in the change; prefer a false negative over a false positive; do not turn formatter/linter-enforced style into blocking findings. The overall_severity score counts only defects that survive this guard.

typos.instructions: Does the changed Rust code have obvious spelling errors at DECLARATION sites (type/function/variable/enum/trait/module names) or in user-facing strings (log/panic/error/diagnostic messages)? Do not report spelling at call sites.

criteria.true: A declared identifier or user-facing string has a spelling error affecting readability
criteria.false: No declaration-site or user-facing typos in the changed code

ownership_lifetime.instructions: Ownership/lifetime defects in the changed code: incorrectly returned references or borrowed values escaping their valid scope; excessive/unnecessary clone() where a borrow, iterator, Cow, or ownership transfer is clearer; interior mutability (RefCell/Cell/Mutex) used without a real shared-mutability requirement; reference cycles with Rc<RefCell>/Arc<Mutex> where Weak should break the cycle.

criteria.true: One of these ownership/lifetime defects is present in the changed code
criteria.false: Ownership and lifetimes in the changed code are sound

error_panic.instructions: Does the changed Rust code call unwrap()/expect()/panic!()/todo!()/unimplemented!() in a production or library path where the failure is recoverable or should propagate via Result? Or convert errors to strings too early, discard them without context, ignore/swallow Result/Option values, or map them to misleading defaults? Public APIs that panic on ordinary invalid input instead of returning a typed error (unless the panic documents a clear invariant).

criteria.true: An unjustified panic, error-swallowing, early-to-string, or misleading-default pattern exists in production/library code
criteria.false: Error handling is appropriate; panics only document clear invariants

unsafe_boundaries.instructions: Does the changed Rust code widen unsafe blocks beyond need or hide unrelated invariants; omit or stale their safety rationale; do raw-pointer derefs without validity/alignment/aliasing/lifetime guarantees; skip FFI validation (null/length/encoding/allocator); or use static mut / unchecked transmute / MaybeUninit / mem::zeroed / manual drop without a documented soundness invariant?

criteria.true: An unsafe block or FFI boundary lacks a documented soundness invariant or required validation
criteria.false: No unsafe/FFI in the change, or every unsafe block carries a sound rationale

concurrency.instructions: Concurrency/shared-state defects in the changed code: holding Mutex/RwLock/RefCell guards longer than necessary (across user calls or blocking ops); holding sync locks across .await; blocking I/O/sleeps/CPU-heavy work inside async tasks; check-then-act races; weak/overly-strong atomic orderings; unsafe Send/Sync implementations that do not prove thread-safety under their invariants.

criteria.true: A concurrency or shared-state defect is present with reachable concurrent state
criteria.false: Concurrency in the changed code is correct, or no shared state is reachable concurrently

async_cancellation.instructions: Async/cancellation-safety defects in the changed code: dropped JoinHandle that still needs to observe failure/cancellation/shutdown; futures not cancellation-safe around partial writes, locks, transactions, or cleanup; async code using sync fs/network/process APIs in request/worker paths that can block the runtime; retry loops without backoff, timeout, cancellation propagation, or bounded attempts.

criteria.true: An async or cancellation-safety defect is present in the changed code
criteria.false: Async code in the change is cancellation-safe, or there is none

collections_perf.instructions: Collections/iterator/performance defects in the changed code: unnecessary allocation in hot paths (repeated String build, format!, collect()/to_vec() where borrowing/streaming suffices); dense iterator chains that obscure errors or side effects; missing preallocation when expected size is known and growth is material; O(n^2) lookups from nested loops where a HashMap/HashSet/sort/index would clearly reduce complexity.

criteria.true: A material performance/collection defect is present in the changed code
criteria.false: Collections and complexity in the change are reasonable

type_api_design.instructions: Type/API-design defects in the changed code: modeling domain states with booleans/strings/raw ints where an enum, newtype, or typed ID would make invalid states unrepresentable; missing From/TryFrom/AsRef/Borrow/IntoIterator where a reusable API needs them; public structs/enums/traits/errors with poor names, visibility, or docs for the crate boundary; exposing concrete collection/sync types in public APIs where a slice/iterator/trait would preserve flexibility.

criteria.true: A type or public-API design defect is present in the changed code
criteria.false: Type and API design in the change is sound

macros.instructions: Only if the diff actually DEFINES a macro_rules! or procedural macro: an $x:expr fragment interpolated more than once so the caller's expression and side effects run multiple times; exported macros referencing items without $crate:: so resolution breaks cross-crate; $t:tt fragments re-emitted without parentheses where precedence can silently change; procedural macros that unwrap/expect/panic on malformed input instead of emitting syn::Error/compile_error!; macro-hygiene breakage (generated ids relying on call-site scope, or colliding on repeated invocation).

criteria.false: No macro is defined in the change, or the macro is well-formed

security.instructions: Security defects in the changed code: building shell commands or SQL by unchecked string concatenation; not validating path/URL/command/SQL/serialized input before use; logging secrets/tokens/credentials/private keys/PII; integer conversion or byte-slicing/length arithmetic that can overflow/truncate/hit a UTF-8 boundary; ad-hoc cryptographic/random/auth code instead of well-reviewed crates with explicit error handling. Confirm attacker control or a trust boundary before reporting.

criteria.true: A concrete security defect at a trust boundary is present in the changed code
criteria.false: No security-relevant defect, or no untrusted input reaches the changed code

name_behavior.instructions: Name-behavior correspondence in the changed Rust code: does each item's name describe what the code actually does? Judge against the item's FACT CARD (name, doc comment, signature, called symbols, return type): a name lies when the called symbols or return type contradict it — a 'parse' that only validates, a 'get' that computes, a 'send' that only formats, a 'load' that returns a constant. Also judge whether the name conveys the item's role — an identifier so abbreviated or misleading that a reader cannot infer what the item does. Judge declaration sites in the changed code only; cite the identifier and line as evidence; compiler-enforced casing is not a finding (rustc owns that).

criteria.true: A changed item's name contradicts or misrepresents its actual behavior per its fact card, or is too misleading to infer the item's role
criteria.false: Names in the changed code accurately describe behavior

comment_rubric.instructions: Comment information-layer defects in the changed Rust code. Comments are the information OUTSIDE the code — judge whether the doc comment carries what a caller or maintainer needs, against the item's FACT CARD: (1) purpose — why the item exists, not what it executes; (2) caller context — who calls it, how it fits the module; (3) caveats — preconditions, cost, what to watch out for; (4) gaps — what is missing or not yet handled; (5) implementation notes — non-obvious approach choices; (6) accuracy — the description must match the signature and called symbols on the fact card; (7) typos in identifiers and doc text. A comment that merely restates the code is not a defect unless it misleads. Cite line evidence. Do not report AI-boilerplate phrasing — the slop_comment rule owns that.

criteria.true: A changed item's comment lacks information a caller or maintainer needs, or describes something the code does not do
criteria.false: Comments in the changed code carry the information a caller or maintainer needs

placement.instructions: Placement and aggregation defects in the changed Rust code: does each item belong in this file / mod / crate? Judge against the file's full item inventory (FACT CARDS): a struct, function, impl or trait whose collaborators are elsewhere; items that cohere more strongly with another module; a file that mixes unrelated responsibilities; a struct that should be split (fields with disjoint users) or aggregated (fields always used together); a trait that belongs in its own module. Judge from the changed code with file-level context; cite file and line evidence. Do not report file length (the file_size gate owns that) or the generic-filename signal (ts_signals owns that).

criteria.true: The change places items in the wrong file/mod/crate, or a struct/trait should be split or aggregated differently
criteria.false: Items in the changed code are placed where their collaborators live

clone_necessity.instructions: Clone-necessity defects in the changed Rust code: a clone() whose value never needs ownership — the receiver is only read, only borrowed, or immediately dropped — where taking &recv (with a lifetime if it must outlive the call), an iterator, Cow, or an ownership transfer expresses the same intent without the copy. Judge from the FACT CARD plus the surrounding code: the clone is justified when the value is stored, moved into a callee that takes ownership, returned as owned, or crosses a thread boundary. Covers the shapes the deterministic layer deliberately does not flag: clone of a struct field (self.field.clone()), clone of a local binding (let s = ...; s.clone()), clone feeding a value only read afterwards. Do not re-report what is already covered: TS-CLONE-OWNED flags clone of an owned function parameter, and clippy's clone_on_copy / cloned_instead_of_copied / redundant_clone own Copy types and provably dead clones. Cite the receiver and line as evidence; only judge clones the change itself introduces.

criteria.true: The change introduces a clone() whose ownership is never required, where a borrow, iterator, Cow, or ownership transfer expresses the same intent without the copy
criteria.false: Clones in the changed code are justified by a real ownership, storage, or thread requirement

cleanliness_semantics.instructions: Cleanliness defects needing semantic judgment in the changed Rust code, excluding clone (the clone_necessity category owns it): (1) recursion where a loop is semantically equivalent — no depth bound, no tree/graph traversal, no early-exit justification; (2) if/else dispatch clearer as a match or lookup table beyond ts_signals' chain detection; (3) concurrency optimization — locking granularity, unnecessary Arc/Mutex, blocking calls in async context; (4) struct field cohesion. Only judge patterns the change itself introduces; cite line evidence; do not report patterns clippy already flags — the clippy gate owns those.

criteria.true: The change introduces a semantically unjustified recursion, unclear dispatch, suboptimal concurrency, or weak field cohesion
criteria.false: Cleanliness of the changed code is sound

overall_severity.instructions: Overall severity of the real defects in the changed Rust code (ignoring advisory-only/style items). 0 = no defects. 1 = minor/recoverable issues only. 2 = at least one likely-correctness issue that can cause wrong behavior. 3 = a correctness defect likely to cause a real bug, or a security issue at a trust boundary. 4 = a soundness/unsafe/FFI defect, or a security issue with a concrete exploit path.
criteria: No real defect in the changed code; at most style nitpicks
Only minor, recoverable issues (no wrong behavior expected)
At least one likely-correctness issue that can cause wrong behavior
A correctness defect likely to cause a real bug, or a security issue at a trust boundary
A soundness/unsafe/FFI defect, or a security issue with a concrete exploit path
